title: Surface Platinum Alloying for Passivation of Oxide Interfaces on Superconducting Niobium Films
authors: Ananya Chattaraj, Conan Weiland, Bruce Ravel, Kim Kisslinger, Sooyeon Hwang, Xiao Tong, Ajith Pattammattel, Andrew M. Kiss, Steven L. Hulbert, Aswin kumar Anbalagan, Andrew L. Walter, Peter V. Sushko, Mingzhao Liu
abstract: Dielectric loss arising from two-level systems (TLS) at surfaces and interfaces remains a primary limitation to coherence in superconducting transmon qubits. Niobium (Nb), a widely used material in superconducting quantum circuits, readily forms native oxides under ambient conditions, leading to lossy dielectric interfaces that degrade device performance. Here, a robust and scalable fabrication strategy is demonstrated for chemically stabilizing Nb surfaces and mitigating further oxidation, including protection of both surface and sidewall regions. High-purity Nb films were fabricated with bulk-like superconducting transition temperatures ($T_c = 9.30\pm0.10$) K. We demonstrate that a thin Pt encapsulation layer, deposited after native oxide formation, can be transformed via thermal annealing into a Nb-Pt alloy at the surface. Spectroscopic and microscopic analyses confirm the formation of a chemically stable metallic alloy layer and its ability to suppress further oxide growth. Ab initio simulations elucidate the atomic-scale rearrangement and electronic structure evolution associated with Pt incorporation on native niobium oxide, providing insight into the stabilization mechanism of the alloyed surface. This approach offers a materials pathway for engineering chemically robust Nb interfaces, including sidewalls, toward higher-coherence superconducting qubit architectures."
summary: This research presents a robust method to passivate the native oxide interfaces on Niobium superconductors using Platinum alloying. By combining advanced spectroscopy and DFT simulations, the authors prove that annealing Pt overlayers forms a stable $	ext{Nb-Pt}$ alloy, effectively mitigating dielectric loss mechanisms critical for high-coherence superconducting qubits.
main_problem: Dielectric loss from two-level systems (TLS) at surfaces and interfaces limits coherence in superconducting transmon qubits built using Niobium (Nb).
main_result: Depositing a thin Pt layer followed by annealing transforms the surface into a chemically stable, passivating Nb–Pt alloy that suppresses further oxide growth.
method: The study combines advanced experimental techniques like Variable Energy XPS (VEXPS) and Extended X-ray Absorption Fine Structure (EXAFS) with first-principles DFT calculations.
model_or_system: The physical system is superconducting Nb films on sapphire, focusing specifically on the native oxide interface ($	ext{NbO}_x/	ext{Nb}$) and its modification by Pt alloying ($	ext{Pt}/	ext{NbO}_x/	ext{Nb}$).
key_observables: Superconducting Transition Temperature ($T_c$), Residual Resistance Ratio (RRR), chemical oxidation states ($	ext{Nb}^{5+}$ vs $	ext{Nb}^0$), and local atomic structure derived from EXAFS fitting.
important_parameters: $T_c = 9.30 \pm 0.10$ K; Native oxide thickness of $2.6 \pm 0.2$ nm; Alloying structures identified as $	ext{NbPt}_3$.
main_assumptions: VEXPS is necessary due to overlapping spectral signatures, and the analysis relies on fitting experimental data against theoretical structural models.
figures_summary: Figures detail cross-sections showing oxide removal (EDX), VEXPS spectra confirming chemical state changes, and EXAFS fits establishing the $	ext{NbPt}_3$ surface alloy structure.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the TLS loss problem in Nb qubits to demonstrating Pt encapsulation. It then uses advanced spectroscopy (VEXPS/EXAFS) to characterize the resulting stable $	ext{Nb-Pt}$ alloy, supported by DFT calculations elucidating charge transfer and structural formation.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses a critical material science bottleneck for superconducting quantum circuits by engineering interface chemistry, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems where environmental coupling (loss) dictates coherence time.
